steps.q: One nurse earns £30,000 a year and one banker earns £300,000, partly because wages, rent, interest and profit are all set differently across jobs and assets. Would you expect everyone's total income to end up equal?
steps.right: No, it would still vary a lot
steps.wrong: Yes, it would even out overall
steps.hint: Wages, rent, interest and profit are four separate rewards, each set in its own market.

steps.q: Two workers apply for the same skilled job. One left school at 16 with no qualifications, the other has a degree and specialist training. Are they equally likely to get the high-paying job?
steps.right: No, the qualified one is far more likely
steps.wrong: Yes, employers only look at effort
steps.hint: Firms pay more for skills that are harder to replace.

steps.q: Two candidates have identical qualifications and experience, but the employer pays one less purely because of their gender or age. Is that difference in pay explained by skill or effort?
steps.right: No, it is not explained by skill at all
steps.wrong: Yes, it reflects a real skill gap
steps.hint: Nothing about their ability to do the job differs.

steps.hint: Look at where price sits compared to marginal cost when there is no competition.

steps.q: A shareholder who owns part of that firm receives dividends every year just for holding the shares, on top of any wage they earn elsewhere. Does this income depend on them working more hours?
steps.right: No, it comes from what they own
steps.wrong: Yes, it rises only if they work harder
steps.hint: Compare a wage, which needs hours worked, with a dividend, which needs only ownership.
